# Family History Handoff: John ("Johnny") Meier, b. 1992

*Prepared 7 October 2026 from the "Ancestry" project, for transfer into a GitHub repository maintained by another Claude session. This document is self-contained: it carries the project's instructions, every file, every memory entry and every conclusion reached in the project's conversations. Where details conflict, both values are given with the preferred one marked.*

**How to read it**

- **Subject.** "John" and "Johnny" are the same person: John Meier, b. 1992, the project owner (GitHub `jjmeier51`). The Ancestry tree calls him "Johnny Meier"; the research reports address him as "Johnny" or "you".
- **Relationship terms.** "5C6R" means fifth cousin, six times removed. "2nd-great-grandfather" means great-great-grandfather.
- **Confidence.** The research reports use three labels: **confirmed** (an original record image was read, or two independent records agree), **probable** (strong evidence that still lacks one deciding document) and **speculative** (a lead only). In the person records of section 3 these map to the schema as confirmed, probable and possible. **Unverified** marks something that appears only in John's Ancestry tree and was never researched, or that research has removed or disproven.
- **Precedence.** The research ran in three rounds, all in October 2026. Later rounds override earlier ones. John's uploaded reports override his Ancestry tree.
- **Living people.** Living people were never researched. Their entries carry only what the project files already record.
- **File paths.** Paths such as `research/notes/round3/meier_line.md` are relative to the project's shared folder `/mnt/project-files/`.

**Contents**

1. Project instructions and preferences
2. Files in this project
3. People
4. Family lines and lineage
5. Stories
6. Sources and research done
7. Open questions and next steps
8. Memory

### 1.3 Preferences and working rules

Each rule below is either stated by John or followed consistently in the project's work.

1. **Uploads beat the tree.** John's uploaded Markdown and PDF reports override or update his Ancestry tree (the Drive screenshots) wherever they conflict. *(John, request 1.)*
2. **Look for standout people.** He wants individuals who stand out: war heroes, celebrities, athletes, politicians and similar. *(Requests 1 and 2.)*
3. **Include distant relatives.** Distant and non-direct relatives (cousins) should be identified and noted, not only direct ancestors. *(Requests 1 and 2.)*
4. **Regional ties.** Ties to **Long Island**, **Northeastern Pennsylvania** and **Virginia** should be highlighted. *(Request 1.)*
5. **Fill gaps and add color.** Gaps in the tree should be filled where possible, and interesting facts about the people found should be added. *(Request 2.)*
6. **Strengthen the evidence.** Probable links should be converted to confirmed where records allow, and new information found. *(Request 5.)*
7. **Push the Meier line back.** The Meier surname line should be traced as far back as it goes. *(Request 5.)*
8. **Pin down origins.** Roots should be traced to specific areas, towns and people in Italy, Germany, England and France. *(Request 5.)* Ireland was added by the research because the Heffernan line required it.
9. **Answer short questions concisely.** A request to "concisely sum up" gets a short answer. *(Request 3.)*
10. **Label confidence.** Every finding carries a confidence label (confirmed, probable or speculative) and a source. *(Practice in all three research rounds.)*
11. **Leave living people alone.** Living people are not researched beyond the names already in the tree. *(Practice in all three rounds; also applied to this handoff.)*
12. **Handoff format.** Completeness beats brevity, nothing is summarised away, the exact eight-section structure is used, long output is split across replies ending "CONTINUED", and John replies "continue". *(Request 7.)*
13. **Section 3 format.** One JSON object per person. Each person is identified by full name and birth year, or "b. unknown". Dates are ISO `YYYY-MM-DD` when exact, otherwise `YYYY`, `ABT YYYY`, `BEF YYYY` or `BET YYYY AND YYYY`. `AFT YYYY` is also used here, by extension. Places run from most specific to least, comma separated, ending with the country. Keys with nothing to say are omitted. *(Request 7.)*
14. **Moraca.** Section 4 must cover the lines Meier, Petriello, Cognetti, Colosimo, Ferlaino, McGuire, Moraca, Fiorillo and Pringle, plus any others. **Moraca appears nowhere in the project files**, which section 4 states. *(Request 7.)*

### 1.4 Conclusions given in conversation, which are not in any report file

These answers were given in the project's research thread in reply to requests 3, 4 and 6. They are reproduced in full here because no report file holds them.

**US presidents (request 3), the concise answer given**

- **Benjamin Harrison** (23rd president) is the **only president related by blood**. He is a 6th cousin 5 times removed (6C5R) through the Long Island colonial lines, via his grandmother Anna Symmes Harrison's Long Island ancestry, and a 7C4R by a second route.
- **William Henry Harrison** and **John Tyler** are related **by marriage only**. Their wives, First Ladies Anna Symmes Harrison (4C7R) and Julia Gardiner Tyler (5C6R), are John's blood cousins. The joke given was "Tippecanoe and Tyler Too": both First Ladies of that ticket are cousins, but neither president is.
- **Theodore Roosevelt** appointed John's 2nd-great-grand-uncle Thomas F. Heffernan postmaster of Wilkes-Barre in 1907, but is **not kin**. Taft reappointed Heffernan in 1911.

**James Clinch Smith (request 4), the answer given**

- James Clinch Smith (1856–1912) was from **Smithtown, Long Island**. He was a socialite who lived in **Paris**, and he died as a **first-class passenger on the Titanic** in April 1912. His body was not recovered.
- His sister **Bessie Smith** married the architect **Stanford White**.
- He is John's **6th cousin 5 times removed (6C5R)** through Richard "Bull" Smith: Bull Smith → Richard Smith Jr. (2d) → Sarah Smith Woodhull → Gen. Nathaniel Woodhull → Elizabeth Woodhull Nicoll → Eliza Nicoll Smith → Judge J. Lawrence Smith → James Clinch Smith. John descends from Bull Smith through Job Smith (see section 4, Smith line).

**When "Mayer" became "Meier" (request 6), the answer given**

- The Munzingen civil registers write the family as **Mayer** throughout (1820–1862).
- In America the spelling drifted. The 1870 census has "**Meyer**", the 1880 census "**Myer**", and the 1892 Hazleton marriage of Henry J. and Annie Higgins is the first record spelled "**Meier**". A later edit to that answer corrected an earlier claim: the 1892 spelling was written by the clerk, so Henry may not have chosen it himself.
- "Meier" is consistent from 1910 on, except for "Meyer" in the 1940 census.
- There was **no formal name change**. Why "ei" won out is a guess.

`````markdown
# Old Records Reshape Johnny Meier's Family Tree

Johnny Meier's tree is most reliable in its oldest generations and weakest at a few 19th-century links. In the Black Forest, his Begelspacher, Schirk and Steiert ancestors match village genealogies built from the Kirchzarten parish registers, often to the exact day. The Heitzlers turn out to have been gamekeepers for the Counts of Kageneck in the Ibental, a side valley east of Freiburg. On the Irish side, his 2nd-great-grandmother's brother went to West Point, flew in Pershing's Mexico expedition and commanded Wilbur Wright Field, and another brother was Wilkes-Barre's postmaster under Theodore Roosevelt. On the Pennsylvania side are an SAR-recognized Revolutionary patriot, Ensign Thomas Lamoreaux, and the likely namesake of Pringle Borough. The Long Island side adds Gen. Nathaniel Woodhull (2nd cousin 9x removed), two probable cousins in Washington's Culper spy ring, and Benjamin Harrison as a cousin through two separate lines. **The link that once looked weakest is now confirmed: the 1850 census of Plymouth Township places Andrew Pringle, age 14, in the household of James Pringle and Elizabeth, alongside his documented brother Noah.** That puts the Lamoreaux line, the SAR route and every colonial cousin back on solid ground, subject to two unproven parent-child links still open on Long Island. The tree also has 30 entries to fix or flag. They range from Mary Connole's birthplace (Elmira, New York, not Ireland) to a "James M. Tuthill & Hannah Reeve" couple that merges two different marriages. The most valuable records to find next are the Long Island compilations that name Temperance Smith's and Capt. John Tuttle's parents. The biggest German gap, Servatius Birkenmayer, appears in no online database at all.

## Black Forest ancestors match the parish data to the day, but two weak links sit below them

### A Celtic town site that stayed Austrian until 1805

The German families lived in the **Dreisamtal, the valley basin just east of Freiburg im Breisgau**. Their homes were the scattered hamlets of Kirchzarten parish (Burg-Höfen, Geroldstal, Neuhäuser, Zarten, Weilersbach), plus Unteribental (now part of Buchenbach), Stegen and Oberried ([GEDBAS](https://gedbas.genealogy.net/search/simple?lastname=Begelspacher&placename=&timelimit=none)). Zarten stands on **Tarodunum, a 190-hectare Celtic fortified town that the ancient geographer Ptolemy recorded by name** ([wissen.de](https://www.wissen.de/lexikon/zarten)). Its Heidengraben rampart is still visible, and finds there include a Celtic mint, ironworking with Black Forest ore, and imported Italian wine ([University of Tübingen](https://uni-tuebingen.de/en/22672)).

The Breisgau belonged to **Habsburg "Further Austria" until the 1805 Treaty of Pressburg transferred it to Baden** ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breisgau)). Every German ancestor born before 1805 was therefore an Austrian subject, while Servatius Birkenmayer (b. 1807) and Maria A. Heitzler (b. 1813) were born in Baden. Buchenbach's coat of arms still carries the Austrian striped shield ([LEO-BW](https://leo-bw.de/detail-gis/-/Detail/details/ORT/labw_ortslexikon/8037/ort)). Just up the valley, the Höllental gorge was General Moreau's retreat route in 1796, and it was made into a proper road for Marie Antoinette's bridal procession ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%B6llental_(Black_Forest))).

### Begelspacher, Schirk and Steiert dates match exactly

The two GEDBAS databases are "Familien aus dem Dreisamtal" (about 30,000 people) and the Heitzmann ancestry file. Both were compiled from parish registers, and both reproduce the tree's 17th-century Begelspachers almost exactly. **Matthias Begelspacher was born 1 Feb 1630 in Burg and farmed the Dachsfangerhof. He married Barbara Wiederle at Kirchzarten on 15 Feb 1654. She was born 25 Nov 1629 in Weilersbach and died 11 Jan 1693. Both people's dates match the tree exactly** ([GEDBAS](https://gedbas.genealogy.net/person/show/1444212307); [GEDBAS](https://gedbas.genealogy.net/person/show/1444212308)). Their son Martin (1656–1711) is listed as the "Jägerhofbauer" (farmer of the Jägerhof) in Unteribental and married Magdalena Lickert around 1700 ([GEDBAS](https://gedbas.genealogy.net/person/show/1444212294)). Martin's son Josef was born 3 Mar 1704 ([GEDBAS](https://gedbas.genealogy.net/person/show/1444212306)). On the tree as it stands, Matthias and Barbara are Johnny's 9th-great-grandparents.

The Schirk and Steiert generations line up as well. Ottilia Schirk was born 2 Dec 1697 at Geroldstal to Christian Schirk and Agatha Steiert ([GEDBAS](https://gedbas.genealogy.net/person/show/1444214156)). Agatha died at the **"Schirkenhof," a farm named for the family** ([GEDBAS](https://gedbas.genealogy.net/person/show/1262182131)). The database also notes that her father's surname **changed from Steinhart to Steiert** ([GEDBAS](https://gedbas.genealogy.net/person/show/1444214165)). Since the tree matches these databases so closely, it was most likely built from the same Kirchzarten registers.

### The Heitzlers kept the forests for the Counts of Kageneck

The Dreisamtal file lists Jakob Heitzler as a **"Kageneck'scher Jäger in Unteribental, Waldhüter"**, meaning gamekeeper and forest warden for the Counts of Kageneck. It also records his role in a 1789 lawsuit and names his wife as Katharina Begelspacher ([GEDBAS](https://gedbas.genealogy.net/person/show/1262173156)). Their son Andreas built the "Jägerhäusle" (hunter's cottage) on manorial land in 1801 and was **Vogt, the village headman, of Unteribental in 1813** ([GEDBAS](https://gedbas.genealogy.net/person/show/1262174650)). Another son, Jakob (1781–1847), was a hunter and tailor who owned house No. 36 in Oberbirken ([GEDBAS](https://gedbas.genealogy.net/person/show/1262175038)).

A farm called the **Jägerhof** ("hunter's farm") may link the two families. The database calls Martin Begelspacher a "Jägerhofbauer" in Unteribental, and a Josef Heitzler bought the property later called the Jägerhof at auction in 1751 ([GEDBAS](https://gedbas.genealogy.net/person/show/1262178929)). If it is the same farm, the Begelspachers and Heitzlers lived on the same Unteribental homestead two generations apart. The registers could confirm that easily.

### Two weak links: a missing Joseph and an unfound Servatius

The first weak link is **Joseph Heitzler (b. 1773)**. The database lists Jakob and Katharina's children as Andreas (1764), Agathe (1771), Franziska (1779) and Jakob (1781). **There is no Joseph**, although the gaps between births leave room for one ([GEDBAS](https://gedbas.genealogy.net/person/show/1262173156)).

There is a competing candidate. A **Maria Anna Heitzler was born 8 Apr 1813 in Unteribental** to Joseph Heitzler (1765–1828) and Maria Pfister (1772–1839). That Joseph was a shoemaker and, **from 1786, the schoolteacher of the Ibental** ([GEDBAS](https://gedbas.genealogy.net/person/show/1420126661); [GEDBAS](https://gedbas.genealogy.net/person/show/1420120011)). This Maria Anna married Johann Georg Gremmelspacher at Kirchzarten on 23 Oct 1855, two years after Servatius died ([GEDBAS](https://gedbas.genealogy.net/person/show/1420126660)).

If she is Johnny's Maria A. Heitzler, the tree changes in three ways:
- Her mother becomes Pfister instead of Federer.
- Her grandparents become Josef Heitzler and Katharina Schlupf. This elder Josef was also a Kageneck gamekeeper, and he is the one who bought the Jägerhof.
- Jacob Heitzler and Catharina Begelspacher, and the Begelspacher ancestors above them, drop out of the tree. Whether the Schirk–Steiert line survives would depend on who the elder Josef's parents were.

Either way, the family is the Unteribental Heitzler gamekeepers. One record would decide it: the 1855 marriage entry, which should call the bride Servatius Birkenmaier's widow if this identification is right.

The second weak link is **Servatius himself**. GEDBAS returns **no Servatius under any Birkenmayer spelling** ([GEDBAS](https://gedbas.genealogy.net/search/simple?firstname=Servatius&lastname=Birkenmeier&placename=&timelimit=none)), and WikiTree has none either ([WikiTree](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Birkenmayer-2)). The only Mathias Birkenmaier who died in 1803 was born about 1718 and married Maria Schmid, so he does not match the tree's Matthias and Caecilia Hohler ([GEDBAS](https://gedbas.genealogy.net/person/show/1013621643)). The surnames Erb and Hohler appear in neither Dreisamtal database ([GEDBAS](https://gedbas.genealogy.net/search/simple?firstname=Magdalena&lastname=Erb&placename=&timelimit=none)). Birkenmayer families also lived in Munzingen, west of Freiburg ([GEDBAS](https://gedbas.genealogy.net/person/show/1370130587)), so the Birkenmayer ancestry may have come from outside the valley.

The tree's "Federer" is plausibly the local Unteribental surname Fürderer/Förderer. The database even records an entry spelled "Fürderer (Förderer)" ([GEDBAS](https://gedbas.genealogy.net/person/show/1444211359)). Kaltenbach is common in the neighboring high-forest parishes of St. Märgen and St. Peter ([GEDBAS](https://gedbas.genealogy.net/search/simple?lastname=Kaltenbach&placename=&timelimit=none)). However, no matching couple was found under either name. One search tip: St. Servatius's feast day is 13 May ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Servatius_of_Tongeren)), so baptisms in mid-May 1807 are the first place to look.

### No emigration record yet, but Wilkes-Barre is where to search

No passenger list, census, naturalization, grave or obituary was found for Freiderich Meier, Maria A. Birkenmayer, Henry J. Meier, William Meier or Florence Pringle. There is one firm anchor: **Addison Pringle's 1943 obituary lists "Mrs. William Meier" of Wilkes-Barre among his survivors** ([Find a Grave](https://www.findagrave.com/memorial/139403232/addison-f-pringle)). That puts the Meier household in Luzerne County by then, so the search for Henry J. Meier should start there.

The likely timing matches the largest wave of German emigration. More than **one million Germans emigrated to the US between 1848 and 1860, peaking at 239,000 in 1854** ([bpb](https://www.bpb.de/shop/zeitschriften/apuz/1848-49-2023/518141/deutsche-forty-eighters-in-den-usa/)). Some Baden communities paid to send poor residents to America: Herrenwies did so in 1850 with the Grand Duke's approval ([Rome Sentinel](https://www.romesentinel.com/entertainment-life/culture/from-germany-s-black-forest-to-rome-a-story-of-emigration-and-survival/article_249f00e6-776a-52d7-b8ee-453efe223532.html)), and Bühlertal sent more than 300 people in 1855 ([Bühlertal Migration](https://www.oocities.org/heartland/prairie/3974/nixon.html)). Servatius died in 1853, when his daughter Maria was about 16.

**Where the proof stops:** the individual Begelspacher generations (Matthias, Martin, Josef) and the Schirk–Steiert generations match the databases closely. The links that join them to Johnny are not confirmed. Those links are Catharina Begelspacher's parents, Jacob Heitzler's parents, Joseph Heitzler's parents and Servatius himself, and all of them need the original registers.

## Tipperary clues, an Elmira-born bride and Pershing's air scout

### Andrew Heffernan arrived as a boy; Mary Connole was born in New York

Andrew H. Heffernan, Johnny's 3rd-great-grandfather, was **born in Ireland on 31 Mar 1848**. His obituary says he came to America "when very young" with "his mother and brothers" and settled in Larksville ([Find a Grave](https://www.findagrave.com/memorial/139403710/andrew-h-heffernan)). It does not mention his father, which suggests Thomas Heffernan died in Ireland or stayed behind. Larksville, earlier called "Blindtown," was a coal-mining borough built around the Boston, Loree, Lance and Woodward collieries ([Luzerne PAGenWeb](https://pagenweb.org/~luzerne/patk/larks.htm)). Andrew's obituary describes him as "an attache of the Court house in various capacities," not as a miner. Nothing in it mentions Civil War service.

**Mary Connole was born in Elmira, New York, on 3 Nov 1850**, came to the Wyoming Valley in 1865, and died in Wilkes-Barre in 1928 ([Find a Grave](https://www.findagrave.com/memorial/139403584/mary-connole-heffernan)). Her brother John F. was also born in Elmira, in 1853 ([Find a Grave](https://www.findagrave.com/memorial/183145812/john_francis-connole)). A 1929–30 county history says the couple married at Plymouth in 1868. It also says Andrew arrived "about 1861" and died aged 76, which conflicts with the obituary's 1848 birth ([Harvey & Smith, vol. VI p. 460](https://archive.org/details/historyofwilkesb06harv/page/460/mode/1up)). The surname Connole is rare and found mainly in Clare, Galway and Cork ([John Grenham](https://www.johngrenham.com/findasurname.php?surname=Connole)). Irish-born Connoles on WikiTree cluster in north Clare ([WikiTree](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Connole-33)).

### Two Boney sisters likely married two Heffernans

The most revealing record belongs to **Anastasia Boney Connole**, who died in Plymouth in 1896 aged 84 ([Find a Grave](http://www.findagrave.com/cgi-bin/fg.cgi?page=gr&GRid=162159301)). Her obituary says:
- She married twice, and her first husband died in Ireland.
- Her children were James Heffernan and Katherine Heffernan Grimes.
- Her stepchildren were Mrs. Andrew Heffernan (Mary Connole), John F. Connole and Mrs. William Dalley.

John F. Connole's own obituary confirms that he was the stepson of "Ann (Boner) Connole" ([Find a Grave](https://www.findagrave.com/memorial/183145812/john_francis-connole)). A WikiTree profile gives Katherine (Heffernan) Grimes's birthplace as **County Tipperary** in 1836, though without a specific citation for the county ([WikiTree](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Heffernan-720)).

The simplest explanation is that **Andrew's mother, Catherine Boney, and Anastasia were sisters who married two Heffernan men**. If so, Andrew's aunt later became his wife's stepmother when she married the widowed Thomas Connole, which would explain how Andrew and Mary met. Three other clues point to **Tipperary as the best working hypothesis for the family's origin**:
- The Heffernan clan is rooted in Owney, in east Limerick, and in Tipperary ([Library Ireland](https://libraryireland.com/names/oh/o-hifearnain.php)).
- The O'Dwyer lands were in Kilnamanagh, Tipperary ([Library Ireland](https://www.libraryireland.com/irish-families/odwyer.php)).
- Katherine Grimes's recorded birthplace is Tipperary.

"Neagle" is probably Nagle, a Cork landed family ([Landed Estates](https://landedestates.ie/estate/2874)). However, the Neagle and Kearney generations of the 1700s have no sources.

### A newspaper family and an early Army aviator

Andrew and Mary had ten surviving children. Johnny descends from the eldest, Catherine E. (Heffernan) Pringle; her brothers and sisters are Johnny's 2nd-great-grand-uncles and aunts:
- **Thomas F. Heffernan** taught school and was a reporter for the *Wilkes-Barre Record*. He became **postmaster of Wilkes-Barre, appointed by Theodore Roosevelt in 1907 and reappointed by Taft in 1911** ([Harvey & Smith](https://archive.org/details/historyofwilkesb06harv/page/460/mode/1up)). From 1913 he owned the *Sunday Independent*, which had a net circulation of 18,777 per issue in 1926 ([Harvey, vol. V](https://ldsgenealogy.com/PA/books/A-history-of-Wilkes-Barre-Luzerne-County-Pennsylvania-from-its-first-beginnings-to-the-present-time-including-chapters-of-newly-discovered-early-Wyoming-Valley-history-Volume-V-part-17.htm)).
- **Maj. Leo G. Heffernan** attended West Point and joined the cavalry in 1911. He earned **pilot certificate #489** in May 1916 and flew with the 1st Aero Squadron on the border and in Mexico during the Punitive Expedition. He commanded Wilbur Wright Field from November 1917 to January 1918 ([Early Aviators](https://www.earlyaviators.com/eheffern.htm)). His father's obituary calls him **"chief air scout to General Pershing"** ([Find a Grave](https://www.findagrave.com/memorial/139403710/andrew-h-heffernan)).
- **Dr. Andrew J. Heffernan Jr.** practiced dentistry for more than 50 years and served 19 years on the state dental board ([Find a Grave](https://www.findagrave.com/memorial/139404421/andrew_joseph-heffernan)).
- **Mary Heffernan** became Sister Mary Antonia, IHM, and taught in Catholic schools in New York and Pennsylvania ([Find a Grave](https://www.findagrave.com/memorial/49215308/sr-mary-antonia-heffernan)).

**Where the proof stops:** Andrew and Mary are well documented, and newspaper obituaries name both sets of their parents. The generations above that are unsourced, starting with Patrick Heffernan and the Neagles and Kearneys.

## Plymouth Pringles: a patriot, a borough's namesake and a son confirmed by census

### Ensign Thomas Lamoreaux arrived twelve years after the Wyoming Massacre

Thomas Lamoreaux, Johnny's 6th-great-grandfather, is **SAR Patriot P-232580**. He served as an Ensign under Capt. Francis Smith and Colonel Woodhull in the Orange County, New York militia, and he signed the Articles of Association. He is buried in Shupp's Cemetery in Larksville, and his DAR ancestor number is A068239 ([SAR](https://sarpatriots.sar.org/patriot/display/232580)).

He moved to Plymouth in **spring 1790** and was serving in Capt. George P. Ransom's militia company by October of that year ([Harvey Book, p. 355](https://archive.org/details/harveybookgiving00harv)). That means the family was **not in the valley for the 1778 Battle of Wyoming, often called the Wyoming Massacre**. Their link to that event comes through marriage. Martha's sister Elizabeth married Col. George Palmer Ransom in 1794. His father, Capt. Samuel Ransom, was killed in the battle, and his remains were later found "with the head severed from the body." George himself was captured in 1780 and escaped from Prisoners' Island in the St. Lawrence River in 1782 ([Harvey Book](https://archive.org/details/harveybookgiving00harv)).

A few more details about Thomas:
- **Origins.** The Lamoreaux family descended from Huguenots who left France after the revocation of the Edict of Nantes ([Harvey Book, p. 135](https://archive.org/details/harveybookgiving00harv)).
- **Pioneer farmer.** He later settled over the mountain in Jackson Township, where the stone walls on his farm were "a matter of marvel" ([Wright, pp. 399–400](https://archive.org/details/historicalsketch00wrig_2)).
- **Davenport ties.** His sister Charity married Thomas Davenport and founded Plymouth's large Davenport clan ([Harvey Book, p. 355](https://archive.org/details/harveybookgiving00harv)). The family was so close that neighbors called their evening gatherings the "Davenport congress" ([Wright](https://archive.org/details/historicalsketch00wrig_2)).

### Samuel and Martha Pringle are documented, and so is their son James

*The Harvey Book* (1899) states that **Samuel Pringle married Martha, eldest daughter of Thomas and Keturah Lamoreux, in 1790, and that both families moved to Plymouth in 1794** ([Harvey Book, pp. 134–135](https://archive.org/details/harveybookgiving00harv)). Samuel built a stone farmhouse near what became the Gaylord coal shaft, served as Supervisor of Roads in 1800, and died in March 1847. By 1873, "heaps of culm" (coal waste) had disfigured the old homestead ([Wright, p. 391](https://archive.org/details/historicalsketch00wrig_2)). An early Plymouth store's account books list Samuel among its regular customers, and the luxuries they record are "rum, whisky, tobacco and snuff" ([Wright, p. 308](https://archive.org/details/historicalsketch00wrig_2)). The family is said to have come from Connecticut, where the name was often written "Prindle," and to descend from a Scottish emigrant ([Harvey Book](https://archive.org/details/harveybookgiving00harv)).

**James Pringle and Elizabeth Croup are documented as Samuel and Martha's son and daughter-in-law** through an entry for their son Noah, born in Plymouth in 1834 ([Harvey Book, pp. 370–371](https://archive.org/details/harveybookgiving00harv)). The Croups were a German milling family from Hunlock's Creek and Nanticoke ([Bradsby, p. 584](https://archive.org/details/historyofluzerne00brad)).

### Pringle Borough was very likely named for Johnny's 4th-great-grand-uncle

A county history says Pringle Borough "takes its name from that of a prominent family of that vicinity." It also notes that **Thomas Pringle was the first president of Kingston's borough council, in 1857** ([Harvey & Smith, vol. V p. 165](https://archive.org/details/historyofwilkesb05harv)). Wikipedia says the borough honors Thomas Pringle ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pringle,_Pennsylvania)).

The best fit is **Thomas Pringle (1791–1861), Samuel and Martha's eldest son** and the brother of Johnny's 4th-great-grandfather James:
- He mined coal in partnership with his brothers-in-law.
- In 1837 he moved to a large Kingston farm. Its lane later became Pringle Street ([Harvey Book, pp. 134–136](https://archive.org/details/harveybookgiving00harv)).
- He is listed among the valley's coal operators around 1843 ([Pearce, p. 380](https://archive.org/details/annalsofluzernec01pear)).

Neither source says which Thomas the borough honors. Another Thomas Pringle, born 1821, also lived in the area ([Bradsby](https://pagenweb.org/~luzerne/bios/wibios.htm)).

The Kingston branch did well:
- **Alexander J. Pringle** (1824–1881) was a trustee and treasurer of Wyoming Seminary, a founder of a Wilkes-Barre savings bank, and an organizer of the 1856 party in Luzerne County that opposed extending slavery into free territories ([Harvey Book](https://archive.org/details/harveybookgiving00harv); [Harvey & Smith, vol. VI p. 378](https://archive.org/details/historyofwilkesb06harv)).
- **Nelson George Pringle**, Alexander's son, graduated from Yale in 1884. His daughters graduated from Vassar in 1913 and 1916 ([Harvey & Smith](https://archive.org/details/historyofwilkesb06harv)).
- **George Lane Pringle** was "killed by lightning" in 1886 ([Harvey Book, p. 137](https://archive.org/details/harveybookgiving00harv)).
- **Charity (Pringle) Mekeel**, a cousin, died in 1899 "in the one hundredth year of her age" ([Harvey Book, p. 1020](https://archive.org/details/harveybookgiving00harv)).

### The 1850 census confirms Andrew G. Pringle's parents

An 1893 county biography (Bradsby) profiles **Catherine Scott**, Johnny's 3rd-great-grandmother, as a working nurse. Born in Kingston on 14 May 1837, she married Andrew Pringle in 1857 and had seven children. She later **sued for divorce and won**, and resumed her maiden name, though she was "better known by the name of Pringle than Scott" ([Bradsby, transcribed](https://pagenweb.org/~luzerne/bios/sabios.htm)). Bradsby lists five living children, and Addison is not one of them.

However, **Addison's 1943 obituary names his parents as "Andrew Pringle and Catherine Scott Pringle, early residents of the West Side."** It gives his birth as 2 Dec 1868 in Plymouth and says he was a superintendent for the Ambrose West construction company and later worked at the Luzerne County Court House ([Find a Grave](https://www.findagrave.com/memorial/139403232/addison-f-pringle)). That effectively settles the link between Addison and Andrew, though his death certificate should confirm it. Bradsby may have left Addison out because he was living apart from his mother after the divorce, but that is a guess.

**Andrew's own parentage is now settled by the 1850 federal census.** Johnny located the page himself on FamilySearch, where it is attached to Andrew Pringle (1836–1900, FamilySearch ID KG4S-XMF). The entry is Plymouth Township, Luzerne County, enumerated 14 Sept 1850 by A. Atherton (dwelling 944, family 964). It lists:
- James Pringle, 51, farmer, real estate worth $500, born Pennsylvania (so born about 1799);
- Elizabeth, 48 (born about 1802, matching the tree);
- Alby, 27;
- Noah, 16, farmer;
- **Andrew, 14** (born about 1836);
- Leva Ann, 11, and Edwin, 9.

The 1850 census does not state relationships. But Noah is independently documented as the son of James and Elizabeth (Croup) Pringle and grandson of Samuel and Martha (Lamoreaux) Pringle ([Harvey Book, pp. 370–371](https://archive.org/details/harveybookgiving00harv)), and Andrew, two years younger, lives in the same household. An Andrew aged 14 in 1850 also fits the man who married Catherine Scott in 1857. The worry that Andrew might descend from Samuel's brother James the elder no longer applies.

The same census page adds corroboration. Two households earlier (dwelling 942) is a widow, **Hulda Pringle, 46**, born New York, whose children are named **Orange, Ransom and Keturah** ("Caturah"). Those names point straight at the Lamoreaux family:
- Keturah was Martha's mother, Keturah (Tuttle) Lamoreaux.
- Ransom was the family of Martha's sister Elizabeth, who married George P. Ransom.
- Samuel and Martha married in Orange County, New York.

Hulda was very likely the widow of another son of Samuel and Martha, which would make her Andrew's aunt. Andrew himself later named sons **Orange** and **Samuel** ([Bradsby](https://pagenweb.org/~luzerne/bios/sabios.htm)), following the same family naming pattern.

To finish documenting this step for a lineage society, the 1860 census showing Andrew with Catherine and their first children would tie the 14-year-old of 1850 to the married man directly.

## Long Island cousins include a martyred general, Culper spies and a president twice over

On the tree as it stands, Bull Smith, John Tuthill (1635–1717), William Wells and Capt. Thomas Topping are Johnny's **10th-great-grandfathers**, 12 generations up, and Francis Brewster is an 11th-great-grandfather. Two unproven links sit between Johnny's 6th-great-grandmother Keturah Tuttle and those founders, and both come from compiled genealogies without primary proof ([My Maine Heritage](https://sites.rootsweb.com/~megen/reunion/ps409/ps409_209.html)):
- **Temperance Smith's parents.** This link decides every Smith, Topping and Brewster cousin. A second candidate has now surfaced (Ebenezer Smith and Anna Smith; see "A rival candidate for Temperance Smith" below).
- **Capt. John Tuttle's parents.** This link decides every Tuthill, Wells and Harrison cousin.

| Cousin | Relationship | Through |
|---|---|---|
| Gen. Nathaniel Woodhull, died a British prisoner, 1776 | 2C9R (also 3C8R) | Bull Smith; Topping |
| Col. Jesse Woodhull, Orange Co. militia colonel, NY senator | 2C9R (also 3C8R) | Bull Smith; Topping |
| William Floyd, Declaration signer | 3C8R (also 4C8R) | Bull Smith; Brewster |
| Selah Strong, husband of Culper spy Anna Strong | 3C8R (also 4C7R) | Bull Smith; Topping |
| Caleb Brewster, Culper Ring courier | 3C9R (probable) | Francis Brewster |
| Abraham Woodhull, "Samuel Culper Sr." | 4C7R (partly sourced) | Thomas Topping |
| First Lady Anna Symmes Harrison | 4C7R (also 5C6R) | John Tuthill; Wells |
| Rep. Selah Brewster Strong, NY Supreme Court justice | 5C6R | Bull Smith |
| Rear Adm. Theodorus Bailey, Union Navy | 4C7R | Bull Smith (via Richard 2nd) |
| President Benjamin Harrison | 6C5R (also 7C4R) | John Tuthill; Wells |

(2C9R means 2nd cousin 9 times removed.)

### The Woodhulls: a Revolutionary martyr and Lamoreaux's likely colonel

Gen. Nathaniel Woodhull was the grandson of Bull Smith's son Richard ([jrm Needham](https://jrm.phys.ksu.edu/Genealogy/Needham/d0003/I2318.html)). He was **captured on 29 Aug 1776 and denied medical care and food, and he died on 20 Sep 1776**. His death turned his cousin Abraham Woodhull against the British ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Woodhull)). He married Ruth Floyd, William Floyd's sister, which made her his own 2nd cousin once removed.

His brother **Col. Jesse Woodhull** commanded the 1st Regiment of Orange County Militia and later served as a New York state senator ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesse_Woodhull)). Thomas Lamoreaux served under "Colonel Woodhull" in Orange County militia ([SAR](https://sarpatriots.sar.org/patriot/display/232580)). The SAR record does not give the colonel's first name, but Jesse commanded the Cornwall-area regiment ([jrm Needham](https://jrm.phys.ksu.edu/Genealogy/Needham/d0000/I2322.html)), so **Thomas very probably served under a cousin of his wife Keturah**.

### The Culper Ring connections

**Selah Strong (1737–1815)**, a great-great-grandson of Bull Smith, was a delegate to the Provincial Congress, a Revolutionary captain, and later a county judge ([Appletons'](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Page:Appletons%27_Cyclop%C3%A6dia_of_American_Biography_(1900,_volume_5).djvu/760)). He was held on a British prison ship ([Underhill Society](https://underhillsociety.org/2017-setauket-pictures)). His wife, the Culper spy Anna Smith Strong, is **not** related by blood: she came from a different Smith family ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna_Smith_Strong)).

**Abraham Woodhull**, the ring's chief agent, descends from Capt. Thomas Topping through Richard Woodhull II ([Stony Brook](https://www.stonybrook.edu/commcms/libspecial/collections/manuscripts/woodhull.php)). However, the sources fetched do not explicitly confirm every generation of that path.

**Caleb Brewster**, the courier whose code number was 725 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caleb_Brewster)), is a probable cousin through Rev. Nathaniel Brewster's son Daniel ([Behling](https://homepages.rootsweb.com/~sam/brewster.html)). Wikipedia claims he descended from the Mayflower's William Brewster, but a Brewster researcher rejects that ([Behling](https://homepages.rootsweb.com/~sam/brewsteri.html)).

### The Harrisons, twice over

First Lady Anna Symmes Harrison was the daughter of Anna Tuthill and was raised on Long Island by her Tuthill grandparents ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna_Harrison); [McCurdy](https://mccurdyfamilylineage.com/ancestry/p14544.htm)). Her great-great-grandfather Henry Tuthill (the Justice, b. 1665) married **Bethia Horton, a granddaughter of William Wells** ([McCurdy](https://mccurdyfamilylineage.com/ancestry/p7701.htm); [McCurdy](https://mail.mccurdyfamilylineage.com/ancestry/g14/p14863.htm)). That gives Benjamin Harrison **a second, independent blood relationship to Johnny (7C4R) on top of the 6C5R already established**. William Henry Harrison remains related by marriage only.

### Founders worth knowing

- **William Wells** sat on Governor Nicolls's five-member council in 1664, served as High Sheriff of Yorkshire (the colonial county covering Long Island, Staten Island and Westchester) and as a justice of the peace, and helped draft the Duke's Laws ([Brooklyn Historical](https://longisland.brooklynhistory.org/stories/the-governors-letters-for-1665-66-67)). He also married Bridget, widow of Henry Tuthill, and became guardian of her Tuthill children ([McCurdy](https://mccurdyfamilylineage.com/ancestry/p16172.htm)). Bridget's grandson John Tuthill Jr. later married Wells's daughter Mehitable, born to Wells's second wife, so the couple were not blood relatives.
- **Bull Smith.** The story that he gained Smithtown by riding a bull around it **is a myth**, according to local historians. Lion Gardiner received the land for helping recover Sachem Wyandanch's kidnapped daughter, sold it to Smith in 1663, and a 1665 patent confirmed Smith's claim ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithtown,_New_York)).
- **Rev. Nathaniel Brewster**, brother of Johnny's 10th-great-grandmother Hannah Brewster, graduated in **Harvard's first class (1642)** and became Brookhaven's first minister ([We're History](https://werehistory.org/harvard-1642-americas-first-commencement/)). Sources disagree on whether he was born in America or in Bristol, England ([Behling](https://homepages.rootsweb.com/~sam/brewster.html)). This connection depends on Hannah being the mother of Elizabeth Thompson, which is only moderately supported.

### New evidence from Pelletreau's *Records of the Town of Smithtown* (1898)

Johnny supplied pages from William S. Pelletreau's *Records of the Town of Smithtown* (1898; public domain, viewed via Wikimedia). They add three things.

**Update (Hauppauge research):** the rival candidate below has since been ruled out. Pelletreau's appendix (pp. 465, 475) states twice that Ebenezer's daughter Temperance married Jonas Platt and died his widow in 1813. The same appendix (p. 479) says James Smith "settled in Moriches" and married Jerusha Topping, and lists their children as Matthew (b. 1721), Ezekiel, Zebulon, Austin, Nathaniel, Francis, Eunice, Keturah, Temperance and Jeremiah, which makes James & Jerusha the only documented candidates. Keturah and Ezekiel also appear as names among John and Temperance Tuttle's children. See the report "Family ties to Hauppauge."

**A rival candidate for Temperance Smith (since ruled out).** Page 46 abstracts the will of **Ebenezer Smith (son of Richard 2nd)**, dated 25 July 1747 and proved 7 Jan 1747 O.S. He leaves £100 each to "my daughters Temperance Anna and Hannah" **when 21**, so his daughter Temperance was a minor in 1747 and born after about 1726. That fits Johnny's Temperance, born about 1732–35. The appendix chart on page 472 shows Ebenezer's wife was **Anna, daughter of Job Smith 2nd** (son of Job 1st). The printed phrase "Temperance Anna and Hannah" could mean three daughters or two; either way, a Temperance is named.

So there are now two candidates for Temperance's parents:
- **James Smith & Jerusha Topping** (the tree's current choice; no source yet names Temperance as their daughter).
- **Ebenezer Smith & Anna Smith** (Temperance documented as Ebenezer's daughter, but not yet linked to John Tuttle).

If Ebenezer is the father, Johnny descends from Bull Smith twice (through Richard 2nd, and through Job 1st via Anna), the Topping ancestors (Capt. Elnathan and Capt. Thomas) drop out, and the Thompson and Brewster line survives through Job 1st. Ebenezer's homestead passed down his male line and was still held by descendants in 1898 as the "Dick 'Nezer Place" (Pelletreau, p. 46 note), so it would have been Temperance's childhood home. No change to the tree should be made until the 1967 Smith genealogy or a marriage record settles it.

**Where Abner Smith's land was.** Page 356 records that Capt. Richard Smith's 1736 tract was left to his son Isaac in 1764, "except 10 acres which he directed to be sold," and that these were "probably sold to Abner Smith." The accompanying 1736 survey map marks "10 acres sold to Abner Smith" in its northeast corner. In 1792 Abner's daughter Juliana quitclaimed to her brother Elisha "all that tract of land formerly my father's Abner Smith, bounded west by the river, north and east by Wm Arthur and south by Obadiah Smith." The tract lay on the **east side of the Nissequogue River beside the "Old mill creek,"** site of Smithtown's first mill, on "the first [stream] south of Nissequague," where relics of the old dam were still visible in 1898 (pp. 44 note, 356). The book mentions more than one Abner: Aaron Smith's will leaves land to sons Abner and Aaron (p. 45), Jacob Smith's 1783 will names his brother Abner as executor (p. 50 area), and "Abner Smith, 2nd" married Nancy, daughter of Richard Smith 3rd (p. 471). The "Abner Smith House on Hauppauge Road" pictured in the 1967 genealogy may therefore belong to a different Abner. The Joshua Smith House (estate of State Senator Joshua Smith, 1763–1845, demolished 1960) stood "in the Smithtown section of Hauppauge" ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Smith_(New_York_politician))); its exact site has not been found. The 1858 Chace map and 1873 Beers atlas of Suffolk County, which label houses by owner, are the best way to pin both down.

**Rear Admiral Theodorus Bailey (1805–1877).** Pelletreau's appendix (p. 472) traces him to Bull Smith through Richard 2nd → Richard 3rd (b. 1696) → Phebe Smith, who married Nathaniel Platt in 1776 → Phebe Platt, who married Judge William Bailey of Plattsburgh → Theodorus. On the current tree that makes him Johnny's **4th cousin 7 times removed** (it would become 3rd cousin 7x removed if Temperance proves to be Ebenezer's daughter). Bailey was Farragut's second-in-command at the capture of New Orleans in 1862. The same page shows Richard 3rd's daughter Sarah married Rev. Naphtali Daggett, later president of Yale (p. 471).

## SAR is within reach now; the Society of Colonial Wars needs two more links proved

| Society | Qualifying ancestor | Status |
|---|---|---|
| SAR | Ensign Thomas Lamoreaux | Strong; every link now has supporting evidence |
| DAR (for female relatives) | Same, A068239 | Same |
| Society of Colonial Wars | William Wells | Best colonial route; needs Capt. John Tuttle's parents |
| Society of Colonial Wars | Capt. Thomas Topping | Needs Temperance Smith's parents |
| Founders & Patriots | — | Not possible |
| Colonial Governors / Clergy | — | No qualifying direct ancestor |

**SAR is the most realistic goal.** Thomas Lamoreaux is an established patriot, and SAR's record lists Martha among his children. All three approved applications (1995, 2014, 2017) go through his sons James or Thomas, none through Martha ([SAR](https://sarpatriots.sar.org/patriot/display/232580)). Johnny's application would open a new line through Martha (Lamoreaux) Pringle and then James, Andrew G. and Addison Pringle, Florence (Pringle) Meier, James Meier and Thomas Meier, with proof required at each step.

**The Society of Colonial Wars** accepts descent through either the male or the female line from anyone who held military or civil office between 1607 and 1775, including council members and justices of the peace ([Ohio SCW](https://colonialwarsoh.org/membereligib.php)). Its women's counterpart applies the same rules and also counts sheriffs ([NSDCW](https://www.nsdcw.org/eligibility-1)). William Wells qualifies easily. His route also gets around the James-versus-Joshua confusion, because both brothers were sons of Mehitable Wells ([McCurdy](https://mccurdyfamilylineage.com/ancestry/p14551.htm)). Capt. Thomas Topping was a captain, magistrate and Connecticut deputy ([jrm Needham](https://jrm.phys.ksu.edu/genealogy/needham/d0005/I2547.html)), but his route depends on Temperance Smith's parents.

**Some societies are closed.** The Order of the Founders and Patriots requires an unbroken male line ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_Founders_and_Patriots_of_America)), and this branch runs through Martha, Keturah and Temperance. No colonial governor appears among the direct ancestors ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hereditary_Order_of_Descendants_of_Colonial_Governors)). Rev. Nathaniel Brewster is a collateral relative, not an ancestor, so he cannot qualify Johnny for the Colonial Clergy society ([Miner Descent](https://minerdescent.com/2011/01/16/societies)).

| Person | Tree | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Henry Tuthill | d. 1644 | Died before 15 Dec 1650 ([McCurdy](https://mccurdyfamilylineage.com/ancestry/p16172.htm)) |
| Capt. John's parents | James M. Tuthill & Hannah Reeve | Joshua m. Hannah Reeve; James m. Rachel Browne ([McCurdy](https://mccurdyfamilylineage.com/ancestry/p14551.htm)) |
| Hannah Reeve's parents | James Reeve & Deborah Satterly | Only Deborah Satterly found was b. c.1705 ([McCurdy](https://mccurdyfamilylineage.com/ancestry/p12609.htm)) |
| John Tuttle | "Capt." | No evidence of the title found |
| Mary (Youngs) Wells | dau. of Rev. John Youngs | Not in the Youngs genealogy ([Rootsweb](https://sites.rootsweb.com/~riss/baldwin/bw/youngs_index.html)) |
| Bull Smith's parents | Sir Samuel Smith & Rebecca Buswell | Unsupported (flagged earlier) |
| Elizabeth Thompson's parents | John Thompson & Hannah Brewster | One register gives Hannah's husbands as Muncey and Samuel Thompson ([Behling](https://homepages.rootsweb.com/~sam/brewster.html)) |

The Tuthill–Reeve error matters less than it looks for cousin claims. James and Joshua were full brothers, so the Tuthill, King and Wells relationships survive either way; only the Reeve and Satterly ancestors are at risk ([My Maine Heritage](https://sites.rootsweb.com/~megen/reunion/ps409/ps409_270.html)).

## Seven records would settle the biggest open questions

| # | Find | Settles |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1860 census, Andrew & Catherine Pringle household (Plymouth or Kingston) | Ties the 14-year-old Andrew of 1850 to Catherine Scott's husband; completes the SAR chain (the 1850 census, found, already places Andrew with James & Elizabeth) |
| 2 | Addison Pringle's 1943 Pennsylvania death certificate | Confirms his parents; explains why Bradsby left him out |
| 3 | F.K. Smith, *Family of Richard Smith of Smithtown* (1967), entries for James Smith and for Ebenezer Smith (son of Richard 2nd); or Temperance's c.1752 marriage record | Temperance Smith's parents: James Smith & Jerusha Topping, or Ebenezer Smith & Anna Smith |
| 4 | Akerly, *Tuthill Family*; Alva Tuttle, *Tuttle-Tuthill Lines*; Baker's study of the Southold Reeves | Capt. John Tuttle's parents; Reeve vs. Browne |
| 5 | Kirchzarten and Buchenbach registers; Baden civil registers (Standesbücher) 1810–1870 | Servatius; Maria A. Heitzler's parents; the 1855 marriage |
| 6 | Henry J. Meier's 1940 death certificate; 1870/1880 census for Frederick Meier | When the Meiers emigrated and where Freiderich came from |
| 7 | Catherine Boney Heffernan's 1904 obituary; Tipperary Catholic registers | The family's Irish parish |

The Baden civil registers are online through the state archive of Baden-Württemberg (Landesarchiv), with image links cited on WikiTree ([WikiTree](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Birkenmayer-2)). The compiler of the Dreisamtal database, Klaus Kiesel, can be contacted through GEDBAS. For Samuel Pringle's own ancestry, a published *Prindle-Pringle Genealogy* is the next lead ([Heritage Books](https://heritagebooks.com/products/101-w0347)). Items 1, 2 and 6 need an Ancestry or FamilySearch login; Pennsylvania death certificates from 1906 onward are indexed there.

## Conclusion

The errors in this tree follow one pattern: **two people with the same name merged into one**. Examples are the two Joseph Heitzlers, James and Joshua Tuthill, Keturah Tuttle and her daughter Keturah, and possibly Thomas Lamoreaux and his son. The safest rule going forward is to treat any match on name and approximate year as provisional until a record also confirms a spouse or parent. The research also shows where effort pays off. Published compilations already cover the colonial generations back to 1635. The evidence that decided whether those generations belong to Johnny at all sat in a few Pennsylvania records from 1850 to 1943. The 1850 census page for Andrew G. Pringle has now closed the biggest of those gaps, so the remaining open questions sit on Long Island, with Temperance Smith's and Capt. John Tuttle's parents.

The German, Irish and Pennsylvania branches all end up in the Wyoming Valley, and the Long Island ancestors reach Johnny through the Pennsylvania one. Ensign Lamoreaux is buried in Shupp's Cemetery in Larksville ([SAR](https://sarpatriots.sar.org/patriot/display/232580)), and Andrew Heffernan lies in the same borough's St. Vincent DePaul Cemetery ([Find a Grave](https://www.findagrave.com/memorial/139403710/andrew-h-heffernan)). The Pringle homestead disappeared under culm from the coal industry that drew the Irish ([Wright, p. 391](https://archive.org/details/historicalsketch00wrig_2)). Andrew Heffernan and his son-in-law Addison Pringle both worked at the Luzerne County Court House, and by 1943 William Meier's household was in Wilkes-Barre. That makes Luzerne County's newspapers and records the most efficient place to close the remaining Pringle and Meier gaps.
`````

#### 2.1.3 `Family_ties_to_Hauppauge.md`

| | |
|---|---|
| Path | `/mnt/project-files/uploads/hearth/66b73be3-517c-48fc-affa-8ff573ff9082` |
| Type | Markdown, 24.9 KB, 125 lines |
| Title | "Johnny's Cousins, Not Ancestors, Settled Hauppauge" |
| Origin | A research report written before this project began, which John uploaded |
| Read? | Yes, in full |

**What it covers**

- The Hauppauge Smiths were the **Daniel branch**, so they are John's cousins, not his ancestors.
- Temperance Smith was the daughter of James Smith and Jerusha Topping. The rival candidate, Ebenezer Smith's daughter Temperance, married Jonas Platt, so that candidacy is closed.
- It gives a relationship table for the Hauppauge figures and covers the Joshua Smith, Caleb Smith and Abner Smith houses and the Blydenburghs.

The full verbatim text follows.

`````markdown
# Johnny's Cousins, Not Ancestors, Settled Hauppauge

**Hauppauge was the estate of a collateral Bull Smith branch. None of Johnny Meier's direct ancestors is documented living there.** The land passed from Bull Smith's son Daniel to Daniel Smith 2d, and then to Daniel 2d's sons Joshua and Caleb. Joshua's house, the "Judge's Neck" farm, the family graveyard and the 1798 mill dam all belong to that branch. Johnny's own line runs through Daniel's brother Job. It came no closer than a 1736 land boundary: Job's son James Smith held a tract that ran up against Daniel 2d's Hauppauge holdings, then sold out and settled in Moriches. The same records largely settle Temperance Smith's parentage. **Ebenezer and Anna Smith's daughter Temperance married Jonas Platt and died his widow in 1813, so she cannot be Mrs. John Tuttle.** That leaves James Smith and Jerusha Topping as the only documented candidates, though still not proven. One finding is new: the Hauppauge Smiths are related to Johnny twice. One link runs through Bull Smith. The closer one runs through his own 9th-great-grandparents, Job Smith and Elizabeth Thompson, because two of the estate's mistresses were Job's great-granddaughters. **That makes Judge Joshua Smith (1763–1845) and Senator Joshua B. Smith (1801–1860) Johnny's 3rd cousins 7 times removed.** Outside the Smiths, the Blydenburghs are the only family deeply woven into both Hauppauge and the Smith tree. Woodhull, Floyd, Platt, Reeve, Tuttle and Thompson appear in Hauppauge only as passing names. No Pringle, Heffernan or Meier tie to Hauppauge exists.

## One Bull Smith branch owned Hauppauge, through Daniel

Hauppauge straddles three colonial grants: the Smithtown patent, the Islip (Nicoll) patent and the 1703 Winnecomack patent. **Its main street, today's Townline Road, is the Smithtown–Islip boundary** ([Wood 1920, pp. 15, 17](https://archive.org/details/historyofhauppau00wood_0)). The name belonged first to the springs at the head of the Nissequogue River. A Winnecomack survey calls them "a place of Springs called by the Indians Happogs." The land between the main river and the "Long Branch" was always called Hauppauge Neck ([Pelletreau 1898, pp. 385–386](https://archive.org/details/recordsoftownofs00smitrich)). The usual gloss is "land of sweet waters." The Long Island place-name scholar W. W. Tooker rejected that reading and gave "overflowed land," for springs that spread out over the ground ([Tooker 1911, entry 103](https://archive.org/details/indianplacenames00tooker)).

**When the town was divided among Bull Smith's heirs, the Hauppauge land fell to Daniel Smith 2d (1691–1763) and his sister Deborah. Daniel bought out her share and left the land to his sons Caleb and Joshua** ([Wood 1920, p. 25](https://archive.org/details/historyofhauppau00wood_0)). The land lay-outs in Pelletreau confirm this. On 10 April 1736 Daniel received land "on the right of his father Daniel Smith deceased," including 493 acres at the head of the river joining the Islip line. Pelletreau notes that the tract "fell to Joshua Smith… and remained in possession of his descendants till very recent years" ([Pelletreau 1898, pp. 236, 248](https://archive.org/details/recordsoftownofs00smitrich)). Daniel 2d's unexecuted will gives "my fourth son Joshua" the Hauppauge Neck, bounded "south by Islip line, west by the river, north by the north east branch," 893 acres in all ([Pelletreau 1898, pp. 359–363](https://archive.org/details/recordsoftownofs00smitrich)).

The Smiths were landlords more than villagers. Wood, a Hauppauge native, wrote that "The Smiths" never built more than the two houses of the first settlers, so the Wheelers and Blydenburghs were "the rude forefathers of the hamlet" ([Wood 1920, p. 16](https://archive.org/details/historyofhauppau00wood_0)). Neither source shows any land in Hauppauge going to the Job, Richard 2d, Adam or Jonathan branches.

**Beware a same-name trap.** Hauppauge had other Smiths who were not Bull Smiths. A **James Smith (d. 1837, aged 95)** came from Lake Ronkonkoma with his brother Alexander, bought land from Joseph Blydenburgh and married Catherine Blydenburgh. Family legend traced them to men who came from England to build Trinity Church. Their line ran to Moses R. Smith and Judge Wilmot M. Smith. A later pair, Zephaniah and Jonathan Smith, belonged to "another family of Smiths" ([Wood 1920, pp. 35–37, 42](https://archive.org/details/historyofhauppau00wood_0)). This Hauppauge James Smith is **not** Johnny's ancestor James Smith, the son of Job.

## The Joshua Smith House stood near today's Townline Road church

### The mansion on the "Judge's Neck"

Wood says Joshua Smith I's house was built "about 1769, not far west of Thomas Wheeler's." Thomas Wheeler's corner was the old store and post office. Four generations lived in the house: Joshua I, Judge Joshua II, Senator Joshua B. and Ellen Smith. Ellen left in 1861 when she married Dr. Jarvis R. Mowbray, and the farm was sold in 1868 ([Wood 1920, pp. 25–26](https://archive.org/details/historyofhauppau00wood_0)). A 1968 Smithtown scrapbook instead dates the house to "circa 1761 or possibly earlier," built as a salt-box ([Colonel Rockwell's Scrap-book](https://archive.org/details/colonelrockwells0000vari)). Joshua I married in October 1761, which fits the earlier date ([Pelletreau 1898, App. p. 478](https://archive.org/details/recordsoftownofs00smitrich)). In 1898 Pelletreau called it "an interesting relic of Colonial days," then owned by Charles Miller ([Pelletreau 1898, p. 236 note](https://archive.org/details/recordsoftownofs00smitrich)).

**The house was demolished in 1960** ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Smith_(New_York_politician))). The scrapbook says it fell to "the onrush of housing developments" despite efforts by the Hauppauge school district and civic association ([Rockwell](https://archive.org/details/colonelrockwells0000vari)). **Photographs survive in the Library of Congress as HABS NY-5414, the "Joshua Brewster Smith House"** ([LOC](https://www.loc.gov/pictures/item/ny0780/)).

The exact parcel is not documented, but the clues cluster tightly. Judge Joshua gave the land for the Methodist church, and his son enlarged it ([Wood 1920, p. 46](https://archive.org/details/historyofhauppau00wood_0)). That church and its cemetery stand at **473 Townline Road** ([Find a Grave](https://www.findagrave.com/cemetery/1978430/)). Joshua also bought "The Judge's Lane," a right-of-way from the schoolhouse to the King's Highway ([Wood 1920, p. 15](https://archive.org/details/historyofhauppau00wood_0)), and the early schoolhouses stood on Townline Road just east of the church ([Patch](https://patch.com/new-york/hauppauge/hauppauge-history-the-first-schoolhouses)). The best working location is therefore the **Smithtown (north) side of Townline Road, just west of the old Route 111 / Wheeler Road corner, near the church**. This is an inference, not a documented address.

### The Caleb place and the 1798 mill

Caleb Smith II (1762–1831) built a house in Hauppauge in 1790, reported to have stood at **Veterans Highway and Old Willets Path, where the Suffolk County Police Fourth Precinct is today**. He moved to Commack in 1819 ([Patch](https://patch.com/new-york/commack/commack-history-caleb-smith-ii)). He gave the Hauppauge house to his daughter Sarah when she married Judge Joshua's son "Major 'Nezer" Ebenezer Smith (1795–1879) ([Rockwell](https://archive.org/details/colonelrockwells0000vari)). Wood credits the "Caleb place" to Caleb I and says the Major's family held it until 1907. That year the Major's son Joshua B. Smith died, **"the last Bull Smith to live in Hauppauge"** ([Wood 1920, p. 26](https://archive.org/details/historyofhauppau00wood_0)).

In 1798 Caleb Smith II, Joshua Smith II and Isaac Blydenburgh agreed to dam the Nissequogue headwaters and build the "New Mills" ([Wood 1920, p. 26](https://archive.org/details/historyofhauppau00wood_0)). The dam formed Stump Pond. The site is now the **627-acre Blydenburgh County Park** ([Suffolk County Parks](https://suffolkcountyny.gov/Departments/Parks/Our-Parks/Blydenburgh-County-Park)) and an NRHP historic district listed in 1983 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blydenburgh_Park_Historic_District)).

### The family graves

**Joshua Smith's family was first buried in a private plot near the house. After the 1868 sale they were moved to the northeast corner of the Methodist churchyard**, where Major 'Nezer's memorial stands just outside the square of evergreens ([Wood 1920, pp. 87–88](https://archive.org/details/historyofhauppau00wood_0)). That churchyard is now Hauppauge Rural Cemetery. Senator Joshua B. Smith is buried there ([Find a Grave](https://www.findagrave.com/memorial/38871768)). Wood does not name the individuals who were moved. No Find a Grave memorial was found for Judge Joshua II or Joshua I, so their reburial there is likely but unconfirmed.

### The Abner Smith House is not in Hauppauge

The "Abner Smith House on Hauppauge Road" in the 1967 Smith genealogy ([F. K. Smith 1967](https://archive.org/details/familyofrichards00smit)) stood on **Village Way in the Village of the Branch, Smithtown**. "Hauppauge Road" there means old Route 111, which ends at the Branch ([Rockwell](https://archive.org/details/colonelrockwells0000vari); [Wikipedia: NY 111](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_State_Route_111)). The scrapbook identifies its owner as **Abner Smith (1734–1782), son of Aaron Smith of The Landing, "an ardent patriot"** who signed the Articles of Association ([Rockwell](https://archive.org/details/colonelrockwells0000vari)). Aaron was a son of Job Smith 1st ([Pelletreau 1898, pp. 44–45](https://archive.org/details/recordsoftownofs00smitrich)). That makes this the one landmark in the story built by Johnny's direct Job line, though it is in Smithtown Branch, not Hauppauge.

## Johnny's direct line came within a property line of Hauppauge, but no closer

| Ancestor | Documented home | Hauppauge tie |
|---|---|---|
| Job Smith 1st & Elizabeth Thompson (9th-great-grandparents) | Nissequogue, the "North Neck" | 50 acres at the Northeast Branch, next to brother Daniel (1688) |
| James Smith & Jerusha Topping (8th) | Smithtown in 1725, later Moriches | A 1736 tract that bordered Daniel 2d's Hauppauge land |
| Temperance Smith & John Tuttle (7th) | Not documented before Orange Co. | None found |

**Job Smith 1st** lived with his brothers at Nissequogue, where the home lots ran Jonathan's, then Richard's, then "the home lot of Job Smith" ([Pelletreau 1898, Intro. pp. xii–xiii](https://archive.org/details/recordsoftownofs00smitrich)). His father's 1688 deed also gave him **50 acres "at the northeast branch, adjoining to the land in the occupation of Daniel Smith"** ([Pelletreau 1898, pp. 58–59](https://archive.org/details/recordsoftownofs00smitrich)). The Northeast Branch forms the north edge of Hauppauge Neck. Job and Daniel therefore held land side by side on the river's upper reaches a generation before Hauppauge had any houses.

**James Smith** was in Smithtown in the mid-1720s, with his earmark recorded in 1725 ([Pelletreau 1898, pp. 82–83](https://archive.org/details/recordsoftownofs00smitrich)). In the 1736 General Division he drew **152 acres "on the east side of Smithtown river, near the northeast branch," bounded south by land laid out to Daniel Smith** ([Pelletreau 1898, pp. 311–312](https://archive.org/details/recordsoftownofs00smitrich)). A tract of Daniel 2d's "at the head of the Northeast Branch, bounded south by Islip line" was bounded on the north "by James Smith's land" ([Pelletreau 1898, p. 361](https://archive.org/details/recordsoftownofs00smitrich)). **James's land and the Hauppauge Smith estate shared a boundary, and the two owners were first cousins.** That boundary is the closest Johnny's direct line comes to Hauppauge. James then sold shares to his brothers ([Pelletreau 1898, pp. 297, 398–400](https://archive.org/details/recordsoftownofs00smitrich)), and **"James Smith settled in Moriches"** on the Brookhaven south shore ([Pelletreau 1898, p. 479](https://archive.org/details/recordsoftownofs00smitrich)). Owning a tract is not proof of living on it, and nothing places him in a house at Hauppauge.

**Temperance Smith and John Tuttle** leave no trace in Smithtown. A full-text search of the 1898 town records found no Tuthill or Tuttle connected to them. The only two hits are a 1704 county highway commissioner and a 19th-century Watchogue landowner ([Pelletreau 1898, pp. 39, 231](https://archive.org/details/recordsoftownofs00smitrich)). No colonial marriage license pairs them ([NY Marriage Licenses](https://archive.org/details/namesofpersonsfo00newy)). The "23 Nov 1752, Smithtown" wedding comes from an unsourced online tree ([My Maine Heritage](https://sites.rootsweb.com/~megen/reunion/ps409/ps409_209.html)). If Temperance was James's daughter, raised in Moriches, the couple most plausibly lived in Brookhaven before moving to Orange County.

No grave of Job, James, Jerusha, Temperance or John Tuttle was found in Hauppauge or anywhere else in these sources.

## A Platt marriage rules out Ebenezer as Temperance's father

Earlier research left two candidates for Temperance's parents. Ebenezer Smith's 1747 will names "my daughters Temperance Anna and Hannah" ([Pelletreau 1898, p. 46](https://archive.org/details/recordsoftownofs00smitrich)). **Pelletreau's own appendix says twice who that Temperance married.** The Platt lineage reads: "Jonas Platt… married Temperance, daughter of Ebenezer Smith, 1st, son of Richard, 2d. He died in 1775, aged 44. His wife died March 12, 1813." Their children included Col. Richard Platt ([Pelletreau 1898, App. p. 475](https://archive.org/details/recordsoftownofs00smitrich)). The Smith genealogy agrees independently, listing Ebenezer's children as "Temperance, died March 12, 1813, wife" of Jonas Platt ([Pelletreau 1898, App. p. 465](https://archive.org/details/recordsoftownofs00smitrich)). It was a close-knit match. Ebenezer's widow Anna married Jonas's father, Zephaniah Platt, so Temperance married her stepbrother ([Pelletreau 1898, App. p. 475](https://archive.org/details/recordsoftownofs00smitrich)).

For Ebenezer's Temperance also to be Mrs. Tuttle, she would have had to marry John Tuttle around 1752, bear his children in the 1750s, and then marry Jonas Platt after Tuttle died around 1770. Jonas died in 1775 with a family that included a future colonel. No source describes her as a Tuttle widow, so that scenario finds no support. **The Ebenezer–Anna candidacy is effectively closed.** It also closes a tempting Hauppauge link. Had Temperance been Ebenezer's daughter, her sister Hannah would have been mistress of the Joshua Smith House, and Judge Joshua would have been Johnny's first cousin 8 times removed.

The other Temperances in the Smith tree do not fit. Job Smith 2d's daughter Temperance was born in 1714, about 20 years too early ([Pelletreau 1898, App. p. 478](https://archive.org/details/recordsoftownofs00smitrich)). **That leaves James Smith and Jerusha Topping, whose children included "Keturah, Temperance and Jeremiah"** ([Pelletreau 1898, p. 479](https://archive.org/details/recordsoftownofs00smitrich)). The circumstantial fit is good:

- Temperance Tuttle named her eldest known daughter Keturah, after James and Jerusha's daughter Keturah.
- She named a son Ezekiel, and James and Jerusha also had a son Ezekiel.
- James settled in Brookhaven town, where the tree says John Tuttle was born.

But **no record yet names Temperance Tuttle's father.** There is also an unresolved chronology question. Jerusha's father died in 1705, so her own birth year decides whether a c.1732 daughter is comfortable or strained ([jrm Needham](https://jrm.phys.ksu.edu/genealogy/needham/d0001/I2549.html)). The 1967 F. K. Smith genealogy, under James Smith, remains the record that would settle it.

## Judge Joshua Smith is a 3rd cousin 7 times removed

Johnny is **12 generations below Bull Smith** and **11 below Job Smith and Elizabeth Thompson**. For each cousin, count their generations below the shared ancestor. Subtract one from the smaller count to get the cousin degree. The difference between the two counts is the number of times "removed."

The surprise is the Job line. **Two women who married into the Hauppauge estate were Job's great-granddaughters through Job Smith 2d.** Hannah, wife of Joshua I, was the daughter of Ebenezer and Anna Smith, and Anna was Job 2d's daughter. Deborah, Judge Joshua's third wife and Senator Joshua B.'s mother, was the daughter of Epenetus Smith 1st, Job 2d's son ([Pelletreau 1898, App. pp. 466, 472, 478, 480](https://archive.org/details/recordsoftownofs00smitrich)). The Hauppauge Smiths therefore share Johnny's own 9th-great-grandparents, which is closer than the Bull Smith link through Daniel.

| Person | Path (their generations vs. Johnny's) | Relationship |
|---|---|---|
| Daniel Smith (d. by 1715) | Brother of Job | 9th-great-grand-uncle |
| Daniel Smith 2d (1691–1763) | Bull → Daniel → Daniel 2d (2 vs. 12) | 1st cousin 10x removed |
| Caleb Smith I (1724–1800) | Bull → Daniel → Daniel 2d → Caleb (3 vs. 12) | 2nd cousin 9x removed |
| Joshua Smith I (1732–1814) | Bull → Daniel → Daniel 2d → Joshua (3 vs. 12) | 2nd cousin 9x removed |
| Hannah Smith, wife of Joshua I (1742–1793) | Job → Job 2d → Anna → Hannah (3 vs. 11) | 2nd cousin 8x removed |
| **Judge Joshua Smith II (1763–1845)** | Job → Job 2d → Anna → Hannah → Joshua II (4 vs. 11) | **3rd cousin 7x removed** (also 3C8R via Bull) |
| Caleb Smith II (1762–1831) | Bull → Daniel → Daniel 2d → Caleb → Caleb II (4 vs. 12) | 3rd cousin 8x removed |
| **Sen. Joshua B. Smith (1801–1860)** | Job → Job 2d → Epenetus → Deborah → Joshua B. (4 vs. 11) | **3rd cousin 7x removed** (also 4C6R, 4C7R) |
| Maj. Ebenezer Smith (1795–1879) | Job → Job 2d → Anna → Hannah → Joshua II → Ebenezer (5 vs. 11) | 4th cousin 6x removed |
| Abner Smith (1734–1782), the Branch | Job → Aaron → Abner (2 vs. 11) | **1st cousin 9x removed** |
| Temperance (Smith) Platt (d. 1813) | Job → Job 2d → Anna → Temperance (3 vs. 11) | 2nd cousin 8x removed |
| Joseph Blydenburgh (1732–1833) | Bull → Jonathan → Deborah → Joseph → Joseph (4 vs. 12) | 3rd cousin 8x removed, *if* his father was Deborah's son |

Daniel 2d was a first cousin of Johnny's 8th-great-grandfather James. Abner Smith was a first cousin of Temperance, if she was James's daughter, which makes him the closest blood relative tied to any "Hauppauge" landmark. These figures carry three caveats:

- **The Job-line paths assume Elizabeth Thompson mothered both Job 2d and James.** If Job had an earlier wife, those relationships become half-cousins.
- **Hannah's path assumes Anna, not an earlier wife of Ebenezer, was her mother.**
- **Every relationship in the table assumes Temperance was James's daughter.** If she were not, Johnny's tie to Job would vanish, leaving only Bull Smith links, and those only if she was another Bull Smith.

## The Blydenburghs are the only other family woven into Hauppauge

**Blydenburgh.** Joseph Blydenburgh, son of a Dutch New Yorker, married **Deborah, daughter of Bull Smith's eldest son Jonathan**, and founded the Blydenburgh homestead at the Branch ([Wood 1920, pp. 26–27](https://archive.org/details/historyofhauppau00wood_0)). The marriage was on 8 July 1692, and Deborah died before May 1699 ([jrm Needham, citing F. K. Smith](https://jrm.phys.ksu.edu/genealogy/needham/d0002/I3699.html)). Joseph then married Catherine DeHart. That second marriage is why Joseph Blydenburgh (1732–1833) has only a conditional relationship to Johnny: the sources do not say which wife bore his father. That younger Joseph moved to Hauppauge, survived a British search of his house for gold that was hidden in a churn ([Wood 1920, pp. 16, 27](https://archive.org/details/historyofhauppau00wood_0)), and is **buried in Hauppauge Rural Cemetery as an SAR-recognized patriot** ([SAR](https://sarpatriots.sar.org/cemetery/display/375105)). Suffolk County calls the 1798 mill partners Isaac Blydenburgh, Joshua Smith II and Caleb Smith II "cousins" without giving the path ([Suffolk County Parks](https://suffolkcountyny.gov/Departments/Parks/Our-Parks/Blydenburgh-County-Park)). In 1790 Washington rested his horses at the Smithtown tavern of the "Widow Blidenberg," Ruth, widow of Benjamin Blydenburgh ([Founders Online](https://founders.archives.gov/documents/Washington/01-06-02-0001-0004-0023)).

**Platt.** Beyond Temperance (Smith) Platt, a Platt also appears in a Hauppauge land chain. The eastern Winnecomack tract passed from Elias Smith to his grandson Eugene Platt, who sold it to Charles Arbuckle ([Wood 1920, p. 17](https://archive.org/details/historyofhauppau00wood_0)).

**Woodhull.** Johnny's documented Woodhull cousins (Gen. Nathaniel, Col. Jesse) have no Hauppauge presence. In Hauppauge itself:

- Nathan Woodhull married a daughter of the fulling-mill owner Elijah Price, and their daughter Maria married James Blydenburgh ([Wood 1920, p. 42](https://archive.org/details/historyofhauppau00wood_0)).
- "Woodhull Smith" and "William Woodhull" subscribed to the 1806 Methodist church fund ([Wood 1920, pp. 47–50](https://archive.org/details/historyofhauppau00wood_0)).

There is a tantalizing lead here. Pelletreau records that **Job Smith 1st's own Nissequogue homestead descended to Job Smith 3d, "and his son Woodhull Smith sold it"** ([Pelletreau 1898, pp. 330–331](https://archive.org/details/recordsoftownofs00smitrich)). If that Woodhull Smith is the 1806 subscriber, a Job-line cousin helped build the Hauppauge church. Nothing yet proves they are the same man.

**Floyd.** A "Charles A. Floyd" gave $1 toward finishing the church in 1816 ([Wood 1920, pp. 52–54](https://archive.org/details/historyofhauppau00wood_0)). He is very likely the Smithtown-born congressman and judge of that name ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_A._Floyd)), but no source connects him to the Mastic Floyds of signer William Floyd.

**Reeve.** Richard Wood of Southampton married Hannah, daughter of Thomas Reeve. Their grandson Theophilus Wood Jr., a Continental soldier, settled in Hauppauge ([Wood 1920, pp. 31–32](https://archive.org/details/historyofhauppau00wood_0)). Johnny's own Reeve link is already flagged as weak, because the tree's "Hannah Reeve" belongs to a different Tuthill marriage. This is a lead, not a connection.

**Brewster.** Daniel Smith 2d married Hannah Brewster (1698–1761), which is why the estate's last master was named **Joshua Brewster Smith** ([Pelletreau 1898, App. pp. 476–478](https://archive.org/details/recordsoftownofs00smitrich)). Whether she descends from the same Brewster family as Johnny's 10th-great-grandmother Hannah (Brewster) Thompson is unproven.

**No connection found:**

- **Tuttle, Thompson.** An "Ezra Tuttle" (1806) and a Daniel and Triphene Thompson appear on church lists with no tie to Johnny's lines ([Wood 1920](https://archive.org/details/historyofhauppau00wood_0)).
- **Topping, Strong, Lamoreaux.** None of these names appears in Hauppauge at all.
- **Pringle, Heffernan, Meier.** None appears anywhere in Wood's history ([Wood 1920 full text](https://archive.org/download/historyofhauppau00wood_0/historyofhauppau00wood_0_djvu.txt)).

## Conclusion

Hauppauge belongs on Johnny's map as cousin country, and the cousins are closer than the Bull Smith link alone suggests. The route that matters runs through Job Smith and Elizabeth Thompson. Their granddaughter Anna and grandson Epenetus supplied the wives who mothered Hauppauge's judge and senator, while their son James held the land on the estate's northern border. It is the same pattern the wider tree keeps showing: Smithtown's founding families married each other so densely that "collateral" relatives turn out to share more than one ancestor. Each new path needs counting before its relationship is quoted.

Two records would most change this picture. The 1967 F. K. Smith genealogy, under James Smith of Moriches, could finally name Temperance Tuttle's father; every relationship above depends on it. A visual check of the 1858 Chace map ([LOC](https://www.loc.gov/item/2013593235/)) and the 1873 Beers Hauppauge and Smithtown plates ([David Rumsey](https://www.davidrumsey.com/luna/servlet/detail/RUMSEY~8~1~217471~5503633)) should show "J. B. Smith" and "Maj. Smith" by their houses and pin down the Joshua Smith House site. A Smithtown visit would take in three places: the Townline Road churchyard, Blydenburgh Park's 1798 mill, and the Abner Smith House on Village Way. Together they cover every physical trace of the family the sources can locate.
`````

#### 2.2.5 IMG_7815, text of Pelletreau Appendix p. 471

> "Descendants of Richard Smith, 3d, Son of Richard Smith, 2d. Richard Smith, 3d, was born April 16, 1696. He married, first, Anna Sears, and had children: Sarah, wife of Rev. Naphthalai Daggett, and Nancy, wife of Abner Smith, 2d. He married 2d, Martha Howell, Sept. 7, 1730, and had children: Martha, born July 10, 1731, married Andrew Sanford. Hannah, born September 9, 1732. Charity, born January 17, 1737, married John Adams. Elisha, born June 5, 1739. Gloriana, born May 5, 1741, married Joseph Bryant. Phebe, born August 19, 1743, married Nathaniel Platt. Isaac, born October 30, 1745, died August 23, 1775. Isaac Smith inherited the homestead of his grandfather at Nissequogue. He married Margaret Theal, March 28, 1771, and left two children: Richard, who married Julia Bryan, but left no children. He died July 28, 1819, in his 43d year. Mary, who left no children. Phebe Smith, daughter of Richard and Martha Smith, married Nathaniel Platt, of Smithtown, and afterwards of Plattsburg, N.Y., Nov. 10, 1776. Their children were: George W., Isaac S., Hannah, Phebe, and Maria."
